For the Gaussian packing in the plot, `{python} appx_gaussian_count_str` primitives at `{python} appx_gaussian_bytes_str` bytes each require `{python} appx_gaussian_mem_str`. A deployment chooses its representation after measuring map completeness, update time, query time, and the conversion needed for conservative clearance.

### Log-odds occupancy and signed-distance fusion {#sec-appendix-ml-voxels}

Discrete volumetric grids model 3D occupancy uncertainty through recursive Bayesian estimation. Let $m_i \in \{0, 1\}$ denote the binary occupancy state of voxel $i$ ($m_i = 1$ occupied, $m_i = 0$ free). Given a temporal sequence of range observations $z_{1:t} = (z_1, \dots, z_t)$, Bayes' rule expresses the posterior occupancy:
$$ P(m_i \mid z_{1:t}) = \frac{P(z_t \mid m_i, z_{1:t-1}) P(m_i \mid z_{1:t-1})}{P(z_t \mid z_{1:t-1})} $$
Assuming that observation $z_t$ is conditionally independent of past observations given the true static occupancy $m_i$ ($P(z_t \mid m_i, z_{1:t-1}) = P(z_t \mid m_i)$), and writing the identical relation for the unoccupied state $\neg m_i$ ($m_i = 0$):
$$ P(\neg m_i \mid z_{1:t}) = \frac{P(z_t \mid \neg m_i) P(\neg m_i \mid z_{1:t-1})}{P(z_t \mid z_{1:t-1})} $$
Dividing the two equations cancels the common evidence normalizer $P(z_t \mid z_{1:t-1})$:
$$ \frac{P(m_i \mid z_{1:t})}{P(\neg m_i \mid z_{1:t})} = \frac{P(z_t \mid m_i)}{P(z_t \mid \neg m_i)} \frac{P(m_i \mid z_{1:t-1})}{P(\neg m_i \mid z_{1:t-1})} $$
Applying Bayes' rule to the measurement likelihood $P(z_t \mid m_i) = \frac{P(m_i \mid z_t) P(z_t)}{P(m_i)}$ gives the measurement odds ratio:
$$ \frac{P(z_t \mid m_i)}{P(z_t \mid \neg m_i)} = \frac{P(m_i \mid z_t)}{1 - P(m_i \mid z_t)} \frac{1 - P(m_i)}{P(m_i)} $$
Taking the natural logarithm of the odds ratio defines the log-odds quantity $L(x) = \ln \frac{P(x)}{1 - P(x)}$. Substituting yields the canonical **additive log-odds update**:[^fn-ml-log-odds]
$$ L_t(m_i) = L_{t-1}(m_i) + \underbrace{\ln \frac{P(m_i \mid z_t)}{1 - P(m_i \mid z_t)}}_{\text{inverse sensor model } L_{\text{sensor}}} - \underbrace{\ln \frac{P(m_i)}{1 - P(m_i)}}_{\text{prior belief } L_0} $$
where $P(m_i \mid z_t)$ is the calibrated inverse sensor model. When prior belief is uninformative ($P(m_i) = 0.5 \implies L_0 = 0$), the update reduces to simple addition: $L_t(m_i) = L_{t-1}(m_i) + L_{\text{sensor}}$.

Along a range sensor ray, voxels traversed before the hit receive negative log-odds evidence ($L_{\text{free}} < 0$), while the voxel containing the return receives positive evidence ($L_{\text{occ}} > 0$). Voxels beyond the return remain unobserved ($L_{\text{sensor}} = 0$). To prevent numerical saturation lockup where an obstacle that was observed occupied hundreds of times requires hundreds of empty observations before clearing, updates are clamped within finite bounds $[L_{\min}, L_{\max}]$ (e.g., $[-2.0, +3.5]$).

[^fn-ml-log-odds]: **Recursive Log-Odds Occupancy**\index{Log-odds transformation!occupancy mapping}: The log-odds formulation maps probability values from the bounded unit interval to the unbounded real line, turning nonlinear Bayesian product updates into fast additions. Dynamic ranges are clamped by upper and lower saturation bounds to prevent saturation lockup. Failure to clamp log-odds values delays the clearing of dynamic obstacles when physical objects vacate the workspace.

#### Octree occupancy and free-space raycasting

Occupancy grid mapping [@elfes1989using] tessellates space into cells and applies this update to every cell a ray touches.\index{Occupancy grid mapping!octree storage} A volumetric raycast walks each return's sightline with the three-dimensional digital differential analyzer (3D-DDA) traversal [@amanatides1987fast].\index{Volumetric free-space raycasting!3D-DDA traversal} Hierarchical stores such as OctoMap [@hornung2013octomap] and OpenVDB [@museth2013vdb] allocate cells only where rays have passed, so storage follows the observed volume rather than the bounding cube (@fig-09-octomap-volumetric-mapping). Free-space evidence lets the map retire a phantom obstacle once the same region is seen empty, while a never-observed cell stays unknown however long the map runs. @Sec-memory-scene-attention-buffers applies this rule to the aisle, where only fresh free-space evidence can vouch that a path is clear.

::: {#fig-09-octomap-volumetric-mapping fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Probabilistic octree volumetric mapping**: A corridor traversal reconstructed from raw point cloud into a probabilistic octree and then into explicit free, occupied, and unknown space [@hornung2013octomap]. The third panel is what distinguishes spatial memory from an accumulated point cloud, because raycasting records evidence of emptiness along sightlines, letting the map actively retire a phantom obstacle track instead of waiting for a timeout to expire it. (Credit: Hornung et al. / Autonomous Intelligent Systems Lab, University of Freiburg, CC BY 3.0)." fig-alt="Probabilistic 3D Volumetric Mapping and Hierarchical Octree Space Subdivision. Empirical 3D spatial memory representation reconstructed from a physical mobile robot traversing an indoor corridor with a tilting lidar scanner [@hornung2013octomap]. (a) Raw 3D point cloud acquired during robot motion, subject to sensor noise and finite field-of-view occlusions. (b) Volumetric OctoMap voxel representation modeling 3D space as an 8-ary hierarchical tree, where occupied volumes are probabilistically updated and stored across variable resolutions. (c) Explicit free-space raycasting and lossless octree pruning, differentiating observed free cells (white voxels) from occupied obstacles (dark voxels) and unobserved unknown regions; free evidence alone does not certify traversability for a particular robot. By maintaining explicit free-space evidence along sensor sightlines, spatial memory actively invalidates phantom obstacle tracks without waiting for arbitrary software timeouts. (Credit: Hornung et al. / Autonomous Intelligent Systems Lab, University of Freiburg, CC BY 3.0)."}
![](../09_memory/images/png/fig09_real_octomap_volumetric_mapping.png){width="95%"}
:::

#### Truncated signed distance fusion

A truncated signed distance field (TSDF), fused volumetrically at camera rate by KinectFusion [@newcombe2011kinectfusion] and incrementally on robots by Voxblox [@oleynikova2017voxblox], stores in each voxel $\mathbf{v}$ a *metric projective distance* $D(\mathbf{v}) \in [-\mu, +\mu]$, positive in front of an observed return along its sensing ray, and a dimensionless fusion weight $W(\mathbf{v})$.\index{Truncated signed distance field!projective fusion} For a calibrated depth image, transform the voxel center into camera coordinates $\mathbf{p} = [p_x, p_y, p_z]^\top$ and project it to pixel $(u, v)$. Its projective sample is $s = Z_{\text{meas}}(u, v) - p_z$. For a range ray, the equivalent along-ray sample is $s = r_{\text{hit}} - r_{\text{voxel}}$; both are positive before the hit. Near the return, the sample is clamped in meters and fused into the running weighted average:
$$ d_{\mu}(\mathbf{v}) = \max(-\mu, \min(\mu, s)), \qquad D_t(\mathbf{v}) = \frac{W_{t-1}(\mathbf{v}) D_{t-1}(\mathbf{v}) + w_t d_{\mu}(\mathbf{v})}{W_{t-1}(\mathbf{v}) + w_t} $$
where $w_t$ is the dimensionless observation weight and the stored weight $W_t = W_{t-1} + w_t$ is capped at $W_{\max}$. Fusion uses a valid capture-time pose and refuses a sample older than the voxel's last evidence epoch. A negative sample just behind the measured return contributes to the local zero crossing under the surface model; it does not certify an unseen obstacle interior.

Interpolating observed samples gives an approximate gradient near a zero crossing, limited by unknown voxels, projective bias, discretization, and moving objects. A projective TSDF is therefore not the nearest-surface Euclidean distance a clearance decision needs. A clearance query therefore reads a validated occupancy or Euclidean signed distance field (ESDF) with an unknown-space policy, the conversion @sec-memory-scene-attention-buffers requires of every scene representation before the permission path relies on it.

#### One frame's update and its memory traffic

@Algo-volumetric-tsdf-raycast applies both updates for one depth frame, and the notebook after it prices the update traffic that @sec-memory-scene-attention-buffers charges against the memory bus. It rejects the frame before touching the map when its capture epoch is too old or older than the last evidence of any cell it would update, then clears and marks occupancy along each ray and fuses TSDF samples only inside the truncation band. Every updated cell takes the capture epoch, not the update time, so a later consumer can judge each cell's freshness.

```pseudocode
#| label: algo-volumetric-tsdf-raycast
#| pdf-line-number: true
#| pdf-right-comment: false
#| html-comment-delimiter: "▷"
\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Occupancy Raycast and Metric TSDF Fusion}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require returns $\mathcal{P}$ captured at $t_0$ in one capture clock; valid pose; occupancy $\mathcal{O}$; metric TSDF $\mathcal{V}$; truncation $\mu$; evidence half-life $t_{1/2}$; per-cell serialized updates
\Ensure observed free/occupied cells and near-surface TSDF samples updated without refreshing unseen cells
\State $(t_{0,c},\epsilon_{\text{sync}})\gets\Call{ConvertCaptureToControllerClock}{t_0}$
\If{clock conversion invalid or $t_{\text{now},c}-t_{0,c}+\epsilon_{\text{sync}}>\tau_{\max,\text{age}}$}
    \State \Return $\text{STATUS\_FRAME\_TOO\_STALE}$
\EndIf
\If{any target occupancy or TSDF cell has $t_{\text{last}}>t_0$}
    \State \Return $\text{STATUS\_OUT\_OF\_ORDER}$ \Comment{preflight before modifying the map}
\EndIf
\For{\textbf{each} return $\mathbf{p}_k\in\mathcal{P}$}
    \State $(\mathbf{r}_{\text{dir}},r_{\text{hit}})\gets\Call{RayFromPoseAndReturn}{\mathbf{p}_k}$
    \Statex \Comment{Occupancy: measured free ray and hit, not TSDF distance}
    \For{\textbf{each} cell $c$ traversed before the hit}
        \State $c\gets\Call{GetOrAllocateOccupancy}{\mathcal{O},c}$
        \State $c.L\gets\Call{ClampLogOdds}{c.L+L_{\text{free}}}$; $c.t_{\text{last}}\gets t_0$
    \EndFor
    \State update the observed hit cell with $L_{\text{occupied}}$ and epoch $t_0$
    \Statex \Comment{TSDF: fuse metric samples only in a narrow surface band}
    \For{\textbf{each} voxel $v$ with $|r_{\text{hit}}-r_v|\le\mu$}
        \State $\text{vox}\gets\Call{GetOrAllocateTSDF}{\mathcal{V},v}$
        \State $d_\mu\gets\Call{Clamp}{r_{\text{hit}}-r_v,-\mu,+\mu}$ \Comment{positive before hit}
        \State $W_{\text{old}}\gets 0$ if $\text{vox}.W=0$, else $\text{vox}.W\,2^{-(t_0-\text{vox}.t_{\text{last}})/t_{1/2}}$
        \State $w_{\text{obs}}\gets 1$ \Comment{dimensionless illustrative confidence}
        \State $\text{vox}.D\gets(W_{\text{old}}\text{vox}.D+w_{\text{obs}}d_\mu)/(W_{\text{old}}+w_{\text{obs}})$
        \State $\text{vox}.W\gets\min(W_{\text{old}}+w_{\text{obs}},W_{\max})$; $\text{vox}.t_{\text{last}}\gets t_0$
    \EndFor
\EndFor
\State \Return $\text{STATUS\_MAP\_UPDATED}$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
```

```{python}
#| label: calc-appendix-ml-tsdf-voxel-grid
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TSDF VOXEL GRID PAYLOAD AND RAYCAST DRAM TRAFFIC
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: \ref{nbk-memory-memory-footprint-dram-bandwidth-3d-tsdf} in
# │          @sec-appendix-ml-voxels.
# │ Goal: Show that sparse allocation shrinks the TSDF payload while the raycast
# │       traversal and its occupancy updates still set the bus demand.
# │ Show: dense and sparse payloads at two pitches, ray rate, updates per ray,
# │       DRAM demand with no caching and at an assumed hit rate.
# │ How: calc_tsdf_voxel_grid_budget (distance-and-weight payload only).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_tsdf_voxel_grid_budget

class AppxTsdfVoxelGrid:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    side_x = 10.0 * meter  # category: illustrative (workcell length)
    side_y = 10.0 * meter  # category: illustrative (workcell width)
    side_z = 3.0 * meter  # category: illustrative (workcell height)
    pitch_coarse = 0.01 * meter  # category: chosen (grid pitch)
    pitch_fine = 0.005 * meter  # category: chosen (refined pitch for tool contact)
    bytes_per_voxel = 4  # category: illustrative (16-bit distance + 16-bit weight)
    band_fraction = 0.03  # category: illustrative (assumed TSDF-band fraction of the volume)
    block_voxels = 512  # category: chosen (8 x 8 x 8 leaf block)
    block_header_bytes = 32  # category: illustrative (leaf header)
    depth_w = 640  # category: illustrative (depth image width, pixels)
    depth_h = 480  # category: illustrative (depth image height, pixels)
    depth_rate = 60 * Hz  # category: illustrative (depth frame rate)
    ray_range = 3.0 * meter  # category: illustrative (ray length)
    band_voxels_per_ray = 6  # category: illustrative (TSDF-band cells per ray)
    bytes_per_update = 8  # category: illustrative (read/write traffic per cell update)
    hit_rate = 0.95  # category: illustrative (cache hit fraction, to be measured)
    mem_budget = 8 * GB  # category: illustrative (application-processor memory budget)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    workspace = side_x * side_y * side_z
    ray_rate = (depth_w * depth_h * depth_rate).to(1 / second)
    cells_per_ray = round((ray_range / pitch_coarse).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    free_per_ray = cells_per_ray - band_voxels_per_ray
    coarse = calc_tsdf_voxel_grid_budget(
        workspace_volume=workspace,
        voxel_size=pitch_coarse,
        bytes_per_voxel=bytes_per_voxel,
        sparsity_ratio=band_fraction,
        block_size_voxels=block_voxels,
        block_header_bytes=block_header_bytes,
        ray_rate=ray_rate,
        dense_voxels_per_ray=cells_per_ray,
        sparse_voxels_per_ray=band_voxels_per_ray,
        free_voxels_per_ray=free_per_ray,
        bytes_per_ray_voxel=bytes_per_update,
        cache_hit_rate=hit_rate,
    )
    fine = calc_tsdf_voxel_grid_budget(
        workspace_volume=workspace,
        voxel_size=pitch_fine,
        bytes_per_voxel=bytes_per_voxel,
        sparsity_ratio=band_fraction,
        block_size_voxels=block_voxels,
        block_header_bytes=block_header_bytes,
    )
    mem_ratio = (coarse["dense_memory"] / coarse["sparse_memory"]).to_base_units().magnitude
    bw_ratio = (coarse["dense_dram_bandwidth"] / coarse["sparse_dram_bandwidth"]).to_base_units().magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(coarse["dense_voxel_count"] == 300_000_000, f"dense voxels {coarse['dense_voxel_count']}")
    check(coarse["sparse_block_count"] == 17_579, f"sparse blocks {coarse['sparse_block_count']}")
    check(cells_per_ray == 300 and free_per_ray == 294, f"cells per ray {cells_per_ray}")
    check(fine["dense_memory"] > mem_budget, "the fine dense payload must exceed the memory budget")
    check(round(mem_ratio) == 33 and round(bw_ratio) == 20, f"ratios {mem_ratio}, {bw_ratio}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    workspace_str = fmt_volume(workspace, unit=meter**3, precision=0)
    side_x_str = fmt_length(side_x, unit=meter, precision=0)
    side_y_str = fmt_length(side_y, unit=meter, precision=0)
    side_z_str = fmt_length(side_z, unit=meter, precision=0)
    pitch_coarse_str = fmt_length(pitch_coarse, unit=ureg.cm, precision=0)
    pitch_fine_str = fmt_length(pitch_fine, unit=ureg.mm, precision=0)
    bytes_per_voxel_str = fmt_int(bytes_per_voxel)
    band_pct_str = fmt_percent(band_fraction, precision=0)
    block_voxels_str = fmt_int(block_voxels)
    block_header_str = fmt_int(block_header_bytes)
    mem_budget_str = fmt_memory(mem_budget, unit=GB, precision=0)
    dense_voxels_coarse_str = fmt_int(coarse["dense_voxel_count"], commas=True)
    dense_mem_coarse_str = fmt_memory(coarse["dense_memory"], unit=GB, precision=2)
    dense_voxels_fine_str = fmt_int(fine["dense_voxel_count"], commas=True)
    dense_mem_fine_str = fmt_memory(fine["dense_memory"], unit=GB, precision=2)
    sparse_blocks_coarse_str = fmt_int(coarse["sparse_block_count"], commas=True)
    sparse_mem_coarse_str = fmt_memory(coarse["sparse_memory"], unit=MB, precision=1)
    sparse_mem_fine_str = fmt_memory(fine["sparse_memory"], unit=MB, precision=1)
    depth_w_str = fmt_int(depth_w)
    depth_h_str = fmt_int(depth_h)
    depth_rate_str = fmt_frequency(depth_rate, unit=Hz, precision=0)
    ray_rate_str = fmt_count(ray_rate.magnitude, scale="M", precision=3, scale_style="word")
    ray_range_str = fmt_length(ray_range, unit=meter, precision=0)
    cells_per_ray_str = fmt_int(cells_per_ray)
    free_per_ray_str = fmt_int(free_per_ray)
    band_per_ray_str = fmt_int(band_voxels_per_ray)
    bytes_per_update_str = fmt_int(bytes_per_update)
    hit_pct_str = fmt_percent(hit_rate, precision=0)
    dense_bw_str = fmt_bandwidth(coarse["dense_dram_bandwidth"], unit=GB / second, precision=1)
    sparse_bw_str = fmt_bandwidth(coarse["sparse_dram_bandwidth"], unit=GB / second, precision=2)
    mem_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(mem_ratio))
    bw_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(bw_ratio))
```

::: {#nbk-memory-memory-footprint-dram-bandwidth-3d-tsdf .callout-notebook title="DRAM bandwidth of 3D TSDF voxel grids"}
**Practical Engineering Question**\index{Practical Engineering Question}: What are the distance-and-weight payload and modeled DRAM bandwidth of sparse vs. dense TSDF representations?

*1. Dense allocation.* A manipulation workcell of `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.side_x_str` $\times$ `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.side_y_str` $\times$ `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.side_z_str` (`{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.workspace_str`) at `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.pitch_coarse_str` pitch holds `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.dense_voxels_coarse_str` voxels. At `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.bytes_per_voxel_str` bytes per voxel (16-bit distance plus 16-bit fusion weight), excluding occupancy, per-cell evidence epochs, and allocator overhead, the distance-and-weight payload is `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.dense_mem_coarse_str`. Refining the pitch to `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.pitch_fine_str` for tool contact raises the count to `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.dense_voxels_fine_str` voxels and the partial payload to `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.dense_mem_fine_str`, which alone exceeds an illustrative `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.mem_budget_str` memory budget.

*2. Sparse allocation.* Surfaces occupy a thin manifold within the volume. Grouping voxels into `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.block_voxels_str`-voxel leaf blocks and allocating only within the truncation band, assumed to be `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.band_pct_str` percent of the volume, gives `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.sparse_blocks_coarse_str` blocks. With a `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.block_header_str`-byte leaf header, the payload is `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.sparse_mem_coarse_str` at `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.pitch_coarse_str` and `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.sparse_mem_fine_str` at `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.pitch_fine_str`. A full map must also budget the separate occupancy layer, per-cell epochs, block lookup and allocator metadata, and capacity for the unknown-space policy.

*3. Traversal and DRAM traffic.* A `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.depth_w_str` $\times$ `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.depth_h_str` depth stream at `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.depth_rate_str` supplies `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.ray_rate_str` rays per second. Along a `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.ray_range_str` ray at `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.pitch_coarse_str` pitch the traversal visits `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.cells_per_ray_str` cells. The `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.free_per_ray_str` cells before the hit receive occupancy free-ray updates, and the `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.band_per_ray_str` cells near the return receive TSDF fusion. Sparse TSDF allocation saves map capacity; it removes neither the traversal nor the occupancy updates. At `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.bytes_per_update_str` bytes of assumed read/write traffic per update, sending every update to DRAM costs `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.dense_bw_str`. At an assumed `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.hit_pct_str` percent cache hit fraction for both occupancy and TSDF updates, the modeled DRAM demand falls to `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.sparse_bw_str`, a `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.bw_mult_str` reduction. The hit rate depends on ray overlap, atomics, evictions, and writeback on the chosen hardware; it is an input to measure, not a property of the map structure.

**Systems insight**: Sparse allocation yields `{python} AppxTsdfVoxelGrid.mem_mult_str` less modeled TSDF payload in this surface-fraction scenario, while bus demand depends on measured locality and on all traversed-cell work. Whether that demand fits beside policy inference on a shared bus is the contention question of @sec-placement-resource-contention.
:::

## Function Approximation and Sensitivity Bounds {#sec-appendix-ml-sensitivity}

A neural network that maps continuous sensor state to actuator commands needs formal bounds on how far its output can move when its input moves. In digital machine learning, small output variations merely shift class logits or perplexity scores. In Physical AI, neural outputs directly command motor currents, joint torques, and end-effector velocities. An unconstrained function approximator can amplify minor sensor telemetry noise into explosive torque commands, exciting unmodeled mechanical resonances, shearing drive gearboxes, and violating physical safety envelopes.

### Multilayer perceptrons in continuous control {#sec-appendix-ml-mlp}

For high-rate proprioceptive feedback loops (such as $500\text{--}1000\text{ Hz}$ quadruped balance, bipedal locomotion, and arm impedance control), physical policies frequently employ **Multilayer Perceptrons (MLPs)** rather than deep spatial transformers. A canonical continuous MLP policy takes a low-dimensional proprioceptive vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_x}$ (joint positions $\mathbf{q}$, velocities $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$, IMU angular rates, projected gravity, and previous action history) and evaluates a sequence of $K$ affine transformations interleaved with element-wise non-linear activations:
$$ \mathbf{h}_0 = \mathbf{x}, \quad \mathbf{h}_k = \phi_k(\mathbf{W}_k \mathbf{h}_{k-1} + \mathbf{b}_k) \quad \text{for } k=1, \dots, K, \quad \pi(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{W}_{\text{out}} \mathbf{h}_K + \mathbf{b}_{\text{out}} $$
where $\mathbf{W}_k \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k \times d_{k-1}}$ are weight matrices and $\mathbf{b}_k \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}$ are bias vectors.

#### Systems profile and roofline limits of MLP policies

MLPs offer a distinctive systems profile for continuous control:

1. **Deterministic sub-millisecond execution:** With small parameter counts (typically $100\text{k}\text{--}500\text{k}$ parameters, or $200\text{--}1000\text{ KB}$ at FP16), an entire MLP policy fits comfortably within on-die Level 2 (L2) or Level 3 (L3) processor caches. Execution on a modern embedded CPU or NPU takes under $0.05\text{--}0.2\text{ ms}$, effortlessly satisfying deterministic $1\text{ kHz}$ control loop deadlines ($\Delta t_{\text{ctrl}} = 1\text{ ms}$).
2. **Low arithmetic intensity at batch size 1:** Closed-loop robot control executes strictly at batch size $B = 1$. The matrix-vector multiplication $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{W} \mathbf{h}$ requires loading each matrix weight from memory exactly once to compute a single multiply-accumulate (MAC) operation. The arithmetic intensity evaluates to:
   $$ I_{\text{MLP}} = \frac{2 \cdot d_{\text{in}} d_{\text{out}}\text{ FLOPs}}{2 \cdot d_{\text{in}} d_{\text{out}}\text{ bytes (at FP16)}} = 1.0\text{ FLOP/byte} $$
   Because high-performance accelerators (such as embedded GPUs or tensor processors) possess operational ridge points exceeding $50\text{--}100\text{ FLOP/byte}$, real-time MLP policy inference operates in the deeply memory-bandwidth bound regime of the roofline model. Total execution latency is dictated entirely by memory bus read latency and SRAM cache hit rates, rather than peak compute throughput.
3. **On-chip cache pinning eliminates memory bus contention:** When weight matrices are pinned in on-chip SRAM or L2/L3 cache, memory access avoids external DRAM arbitration entirely. Reading from off-chip LPDDR DRAM subjects inference to variable memory bus contention from concurrent camera direct memory access (DMA) transactions and display pipelines, introducing latency jitter of $\pm 20\text{--}50\text{ }\mu\text{s}$. In contrast, cache-resident MLPs execute with sub-microsecond timing variance ($\le 5\text{ }\mu\text{s}$), making them suitable for hard real-time execution inside kernel interrupt handlers or PREEMPT_RT threads.
4. **Negligible activation memory footprint:** Unlike spatial transformers where self-attention matrices scale quadratically ($\mathcal{O}(N^2)$) in visual token count, an MLP policy processes low-dimensional state vectors $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_x}$. Hidden activations require storing only $\mathbf{h}_k \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}$ (typically $256\text{--}512$ scalar values, or $512\text{--}1024\text{ bytes}$ at FP16). The total working set memory footprint across all layers is under $16\text{ KB}$, enabling static stack allocation at boot time with zero dynamic heap allocations (`malloc`/`free`) during real-time control cycles.

### Lipschitz continuity and spectral normalization {#sec-appendix-ml-lipschitz}

A neural policy $\pi: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{U}$ is $L$-Lipschitz continuous if there exists a non-negative scalar constant $L$ such that for all $\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2 \in \mathcal{X}$:\index{Lipschitz continuity!spectral normalization}
$$ \| \pi(\mathbf{x}_1) - \pi(\mathbf{x}_2) \|_{\mathcal{U}} \le L \| \mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{x}_2 \|_{\mathcal{X}} $$
For a feedforward network with $K$ layers $\pi(\mathbf{x}) = \phi_K(\mathbf{W}_K \dots \phi_1(\mathbf{W}_1 \mathbf{x}))$, let $L_{\phi_k}$ bound each activation's slope over the input domain. The composed Lipschitz bound is:
$$ L \le \prod_{k=1}^K L_{\phi_k} \| \mathbf{W}_k \|_2 $$
where $\|\mathbf{W}_k\|_2 = \sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{W}_k)$ is the spectral norm (the largest singular value of weight matrix $\mathbf{W}_k$). Standard activations such as ReLU and Tanh are 1-Lipschitz in their scalar forms; exact GeLU has maximum derivative about $1.1289$, so assigning it a factor of one would understate the bound.

If each layer in a 4-layer MLP has spectral norm $\|\mathbf{W}_k\|_2 \approx 3.0$, the overall network Lipschitz constant compounds exponentially to $L \approx 3^4 = 81$. A modest $1\text{ mm}$ position measurement error can produce an $81\text{ mm}$ displacement or an $81\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ torque transient, commanding extreme actuator forces that violate joint limits.

To bound policy sensitivity directly during training, **spectral normalization** reparameterizes each weight matrix by its spectral norm:
$$ \overline{\mathbf{W}}_k = \frac{\mathbf{W}_k}{\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{W}_k)} $$
where $\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{W}_k)$ is estimated efficiently via power iteration during forward passes. Spectral normalization strictly forces $\|\overline{\mathbf{W}}_k\|_2 = 1$, ensuring that the global Lipschitz constant cannot exceed $L \le \prod_{k=1}^K L_{\phi_k}$, preventing unconstrained gradient explosion and stabilizing continuous control policies.

### Perturbation amplification and supervisory clamping

In physical systems, input state $\mathbf{x}$ is corrupted by sensor measurement noise $\delta \mathbf{x}$ bounded by $\|\delta \mathbf{x}\| \le \epsilon$. The resulting deviation in commanded control action is bounded by:
$$ \| \delta \mathbf{u} \| = \| \pi(\mathbf{x} + \delta \mathbf{x}) - \pi(\mathbf{x}) \| \le L \epsilon $$
The constant has output-units per input-unit. For an illustrative policy mapping position in meters to torque in newton-meters, $L=10^3\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}/\text{m}$ and $\epsilon=1\text{ mm}$ allow up to $1\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ of command change. Whether that exceeds torque headroom depends on the joint and operating state. Spectral normalization can reduce an upper bound on network sensitivity. It bounds the network, not the plant, so stability, safe torque, and sensor validity still come from a separate actuator limit and a state-dependent permission check.

## Imitation Learning and Compounding Covariate Shift {#sec-appendix-ml-compounding}

Behavioral cloning frames physical policy acquisition as supervised regression over demonstrator state-action pairs.

### Mode averaging and the decoders that avoid it {#sec-appendix-ml-multimodal}

Consider an imitation learning objective minimizing mean squared error ($L_2$ loss) over demonstration distribution $P(o, a)$:\index{Mode averaging!appendix refresher}
$$ \min_\pi \mathbb{E}_{(o, a) \sim \mathcal{D}} \left[ \| a - \pi(o) \|_2^2 \right] $$
By the law of total expectation, decomposing the error around the conditional mean $\mathbb{E}[a \mid o]$ yields an orthogonal variance decomposition:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}_{a \mid o} \left[ \| a - \pi(o) \|_2^2 \mid o \right] &= \mathbb{E}_{a \mid o} \left[ \| (a - \mathbb{E}[a \mid o]) + (\mathbb{E}[a \mid o] - \pi(o)) \|_2^2 \mid o \right] \\
&= \mathbb{E}_{a \mid o} \left[ \| a - \mathbb{E}[a \mid o] \|_2^2 \mid o \right] + \| \mathbb{E}[a \mid o] - \pi(o) \|_2^2 \\
&\quad + 2 \left\langle \mathbb{E}_{a \mid o}[a - \mathbb{E}[a \mid o] \mid o], \, \mathbb{E}[a \mid o] - \pi(o) \right\rangle
\end{aligned}
$$
Because $\mathbb{E}_{a \mid o}[a - \mathbb{E}[a \mid o] \mid o] = \mathbf{0}$, the cross-term vanishes identically, leaving:
$$ \mathbb{E}_{(o, a) \sim \mathcal{D}} \left[ \| a - \pi(o) \|_2^2 \right] = \mathbb{E}_o \left[ \operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Cov}(a \mid o)) \right] + \mathbb{E}_o \left[ \| \mathbb{E}[a \mid o] - \pi(o) \|_2^2 \right] $$
The first term is the irreducible conditional variance of demonstrator behavior. The second term is non-negative and strictly minimized if and only if the policy evaluates to the **conditional expectation**:
$$ \pi^*(o) = \mathbb{E}[a \mid o] = \int_{\mathcal{A}} a P(a \mid o) \, da $$
In digital machine learning tasks (such as computer vision regression), predicting the conditional expectation over ambiguous targets produces a blurry reconstruction—a soft pixel average that remains safely confined to software memory. In Physical AI systems, commanded actions cross the causal boundary into continuous Euclidean space governed by non-convex obstacles, joint limits, and irreversible contact dynamics.

Demonstrator behavior in physical manipulation and navigation is inherently multimodal:

- Dodging an obstacle: an expert steers left ($a = +1.0$) or right ($a = -1.0$) around a central pillar with equal probability $P(a = +1 \mid o) = P(a = -1 \mid o) = 0.5$.
- Symmetrical manipulation: an end effector approaches a cylindrical object from azimuth $\theta = 0^\circ$ or $\theta = 180^\circ$.
- Assembly routing: threading a flexible cable clockwise or counter-clockwise around a structural fastener.

Because demonstration density $P(a \mid o)$ is supported on disjoint, disconnected modes separated by an obstacle, the conditional expectation computes the arithmetic mean:
$$ \pi^*(o) = 0.5(+1.0) + 0.5(-1.0) = 0.0 $$
This mean action lies in a region of zero demonstration probability ($P(a = 0.0 \mid o) = 0$). In the physical workspace, the coordinate $a = 0.0$ corresponds precisely to the geometric position of the central obstacle. Commanding $\pi^*(o) = 0.0$ instructs the steering actuator to hold dead center at full cruising speed, driving the physical robot directly into the pillar. In physical autonomy, regression mode averaging does not produce a cosmetic blur; it commands an irreversible, lethal collision.

#### Decoder families

A decoder avoids mode averaging by parameterizing the conditional action distribution $P(a \mid o)$ rather than its expectation. The families below trade inference cost against distributional expressiveness; none of them supplies recovery states that the demonstrations lack. @Sec-training-synthesis-regimes compares them by the network evaluations each chunk costs, which is where the choice reaches the control deadline.\index{Action decoder!multimodal families}

1. **Deterministic direct regression (MLP).** A feedforward multilayer perceptron directly predicts action $\hat{a} = \pi_\theta(o)$ via $L_2$ regression. As proved by the conditional expectation derivation above, minimizing mean squared error under multimodal demonstration distributions forces the network to output the arithmetic mean of all valid behaviors, driving the physical robot into obstacles located between demonstrated modes. While MLPs evaluate in $< 0.1\text{ ms}$ ($\mathcal{O}(1)$ forward pass) with minimal memory footprint, their expressive capacity is strictly unimodal.
2. **Mixture density networks.** A Gaussian mixture model (GMM) head parameterizes policy output as a conditional mixture of $M$ Gaussian components:
   $$ \pi(a \mid o) = \sum_{m=1}^M w_m(o) \, \mathcal{N}\left(\mu_m(o), \Sigma_m(o)\right) $$
   where the network predicts mixture weights $w_m(o)$, component means $\mu_m(o)$, and covariances $\Sigma_m(o)$. It yields closed-form log-likelihood and exact densities in a single forward pass. However, maximum-likelihood training suffers from mode collapse and covariance singularities, the architecture scales poorly to high-dimensional multi-step trajectory chunks, and fixed component count $M$ fails when demonstrations branch unevenly.

3. **Implicit behavioral cloning.** Implicit behavioral cloning (IBC) [@florence2022implicit] learns an energy-based model $E_\theta(o, a) \in \mathbb{R}$, trained with contrastive or InfoNCE objectives to assign low energy to demonstrated state-action pairs and high energy to counterfactual actions. Inference solves
   $$ a^* = \arg\min_a E_\theta(o, a) $$
   Energy formulations represent discontinuous, sharply multimodal distributions and non-convex boundaries that a continuous feedforward map cannot. Inference requires iterative derivative-free or gradient-based optimization whose latency and convergence depend on sample counts and accelerator parallelism, with risks of settling into suboptimal local energy minima.

4. **Conditional diffusion and flow matching.** Diffusion Policy [@chi2024diffusionpolicy] and flow-matching decoders generate entire action trajectory chunks via iterative denoising or ordinary differential equation (ODE) integration. Their training targets injected noise vectors or continuous velocity fields conditioned on corrupted states, observations, and timesteps rather than clean actions, completely circumventing conditional expectation averaging. @Sec-appendix-ml-diffusion derives both objectives and prices their sampling steps.
5. **Latent-variable chunking.** Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) [@zhao2023learning] predicts an action trajectory chunk $\mathbf{A}_t = (\mathbf{a}_t, \mathbf{a}_{t+1}, \dots, \mathbf{a}_{t+H_a-1}) \in \mathbb{R}^{H_a \times D_a}$ from observation $\mathbf{o}_t$ using a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE). The true objective is to maximize the conditional log-marginal likelihood of demonstrated chunks across dataset $\mathcal{D}$:
   $$ \ln p_\theta(\mathbf{A}_t \mid \mathbf{o}_t) = \ln \int_{\mathcal{Z}} p_\theta(\mathbf{A}_t, \mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t) \, d\mathbf{z} $$
   Because this marginalization is intractable, ACT introduces a variational posterior $q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t)$ parameterized by a transformer encoder. Expanding the identity with $p_\theta(\mathbf{A}_t, \mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t) = p_\theta(\mathbf{A}_t \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{z}) p(\mathbf{z})$:
   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   \ln p_\theta(\mathbf{A}_t \mid \mathbf{o}_t) &= \int_{\mathcal{Z}} q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t) \ln p_\theta(\mathbf{A}_t \mid \mathbf{o}_t) \, d\mathbf{z} \\
   &= \int_{\mathcal{Z}} q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t) \ln \left( \frac{p_\theta(\mathbf{A}_t, \mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t)}{q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t)} \cdot \frac{q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t)}{p_\theta(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t)} \right) d\mathbf{z} \\
   &= \int_{\mathcal{Z}} q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t) \ln \frac{p_\theta(\mathbf{A}_t, \mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t)}{q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t)} \, d\mathbf{z} + \int_{\mathcal{Z}} q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t) \ln \frac{q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t)}{p_\theta(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t)} \, d\mathbf{z} \\
   &= \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t)} \left[ \ln \frac{p_\theta(\mathbf{A}_t \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{z}) p(\mathbf{z})}{q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t)} \right] + D_{\text{KL}}\left( q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t) \,\parallel\, p_\theta(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t) \right) \\
   &\ge \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t)} \left[ \ln p_\theta(\mathbf{A}_t \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{z}) \right] - D_{\text{KL}}\left( q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t) \,\parallel\, p(\mathbf{z}) \right) \equiv \mathcal{L}_{\text{ELBO}}(\theta, \phi)
   \end{aligned}
   $$
   Assuming standard isotropic Gaussian prior $p(\mathbf{z}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}_{d_z})$ and diagonal Gaussian variational posterior $q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t) = \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_\phi, \operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}_\phi^2))$, the Kullback-Leibler divergence evaluates in closed form:
   $$ D_{\text{KL}}\left( q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t) \,\parallel\, \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}) \right) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{j=1}^{d_z} \left( \sigma_{\phi, j}^2 + \mu_{\phi, j}^2 - 1 - \ln(\sigma_{\phi, j}^2) \right) $$
   Sampling directly as $\mathbf{z} \sim q_\phi$ is a stochastic operation that prevents backpropagation because the node has no analytical derivatives with respect to encoder parameters $\phi$. ACT resolves this via the **reparameterization trick**: isolating stochasticity into parameter-free standard normal noise $\boldsymbol{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}_{d_z})$:
   $$ \mathbf{z} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_\phi(\mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t) + \boldsymbol{\sigma}_\phi(\mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t) \odot \boldsymbol{\epsilon}, \quad \text{yielding } \frac{\partial \mathbf{z}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}_\phi} = \mathbf{I}, \quad \frac{\partial \mathbf{z}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\sigma}_\phi} = \operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) $$
   To parameterize the reconstruction likelihood, ACT models $p_\theta(\mathbf{A}_t \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{z})$ as an isotropic Laplace distribution:
   $$ p_\theta(\mathbf{A}_t \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{z}) = \frac{1}{(2b)^{H_a D_a}} \exp\left( -\frac{\|\mathbf{A}_t - \pi_\theta(\mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{z})\|_1}{b} \right) $$
   Maximizing the log-likelihood is equivalent to minimizing the $L_1$ norm $\|\mathbf{A}_t - \pi_\theta(\mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{z})\|_1$. For physical robot teleoperation, $L_1$ loss provides constant-magnitude error gradients that avoid over-penalizing high-frequency human demonstrator sub-movements and velocity tremors, which Gaussian $L_2$ regression squares and overfits. Weighting the KL regularizer by hyperparameter $\beta > 0$ yields the full training loss:
   $$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{ACT}}(\theta, \phi) = \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t) \sim \mathcal{D}, \boldsymbol{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})} \left[ \|\mathbf{A}_t - \pi_\theta(\mathbf{o}_t, \boldsymbol{\mu}_\phi + \boldsymbol{\sigma}_\phi \odot \boldsymbol{\epsilon})\|_1 \right] + \beta D_{\text{KL}}\left( q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t) \,\parallel\, \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}) \right) $$

   The latent variable $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_z}$ acts as a continuous style and intention selector: distinct demonstration modes (such as reaching left versus right around an obstacle) map to separated clusters in latent space. The decoder uses learned temporal positional queries to generate all $H_a$ steps simultaneously, with multi-head self-attention attending across the chunk to enforce kinematic smoothness. Action chunking fundamentally alters compounding covariate shift: in single-step imitation ($H_a = 1$), an error at any step perturbs the plant state into off-distribution regions, accumulating error quadratically as $\mathcal{O}(T^2 \epsilon)$ over horizon $T$ (derived later in this section). By generating an entire coherent trajectory chunk $\mathbf{A}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{H_a \times D_a}$ at once, ACT reduces the count of closed-loop policy intervention boundaries across horizon $T$ by a factor of $H_a$. Within the chunk, self-attention across query tokens enforces kinematic smoothness, dampening compounding error accumulation from $\mathcal{O}(T^2 \epsilon)$ to $\mathcal{O}((T / H_a)^2 \epsilon_{\text{chunk}})$.

   Crucially for real-time systems, at test time the encoder $q_\phi$ (which requires unobserved future actions $\mathbf{A}_t$) is discarded. Setting $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{0}$ (the deterministic mean of the prior) conditions decoder $\pi_\theta$ on the dominant demonstrated style, evaluating the entire $H_a$-step chunk in a **single forward pass** ($\mathcal{O}(1)$ network evaluations, typically $15\text{--}25\text{ ms}$ on embedded accelerators). With a parameter footprint of $80\text{--}150\text{ MB}$ at FP16 and high sample efficiency ($50\text{--}100$ demonstrations suffice for bi-manual manipulation), ACT provides an attractive systems profile. However, setting $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{0}$ collapses multimodal coverage to a single dominant mode during physical execution; sampling $\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$ risks drawing unpopulated latent regions between demonstrated modes. To prevent discontinuous setpoint jumps between consecutive chunks, ACT blurs receding-horizon predictions via **temporal ensembling**:
   $$ \mathbf{a}_t = \frac{\sum_{i=0}^{\min(t, H_a-1)} w_i \, \mathbf{A}_{t-i}[i]}{\sum_{i=0}^{\min(t, H_a-1)} w_i}, \qquad w_i = \exp(-m \cdot i) $$
   where $m > 0$ controls exponential decay weighting across overlapping historical predictions.

6. **Discrete action tokens.** Vision-language-action models such as RT-1, RT-2, and OpenVLA [@brohan2023rt1; @brohan2023rt2; @kim2024openvla] discretize continuous action dimensions into $B$ uniform bins (commonly 256) and emit categorical tokens:
   $$ \text{bin}(a_k) = \left\lfloor \frac{a_k - a_{\min}}{a_{\max} - a_{\min}} \times (B - 1) \right\rfloor $$
   Discretization avoids mode averaging by modeling categorical probabilities over token bins, reusing language model classification heads. However, it incurs quantization error $\Delta a = (a_{\max} - a_{\min})/B$ and requires $D_a$ autoregressive token prediction steps per action vector, scaling inference latency linearly with action dimensionality.

### Continuous trajectory diffusion and flow matching {#sec-appendix-ml-diffusion}

Continuous trajectory diffusion treats policy synthesis as generative denoising over continuous multi-step action trajectory chunks $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times D_a}$ conditioned on visual and proprioceptive observation histories $\mathbf{O}$ [@chi2024diffusionpolicy]. Rather than predicting an unconstrained point estimate via mean squared error, diffusion models represent complex multimodal action distributions without collapsing into mode averaging.\index{Diffusion policy!score-matching derivation}\index{Continuous flow matching!vector field regression}

The noise-prediction backbone $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta$ is typically implemented using either a 1D Temporal Convolutional (Conv1D) U-Net or a Diffusion Transformer (DiT):

- **1D Temporal Convolutional U-Net:** Applies hierarchical 1D convolutions across the action chunk time horizon, modulating intermediate features via FiLM (Feature-wise Linear Modulation) conditioning on visual tokens and diffusion step embeddings. With small parameter counts (typically $48\text{M}$ parameters, $96\text{ MB}$ at FP16), Conv1D U-Nets stream intermediate feature activations through on-chip accelerator SRAM line buffers ($< 2\text{ MB}$), eliminating off-chip DRAM activation traffic and maintaining fast, deterministic execution times ($1.5\text{--}2.5\text{ ms}$ per step).
- **Diffusion Transformer (DiT):** Treats each trajectory timestep as a continuous token, processing action tokens with self-attention and cross-attending to visual conditioning. While DiTs scale effectively to complex multi-task foundation models, computing multi-head self-attention across trajectory tokens expands the activation memory footprint and increases parameter sizes ($150\text{--}300\text{M}$ parameters, $300\text{--}600\text{ MB}$ at FP16), stressing memory bandwidth and pushing per-step latency to $5\text{--}10\text{ ms}$.

@Fig-diffusion-policy-architecture shows the policy's structure. It conditions on a short history of camera images and robot state, denoises a candidate chunk from Gaussian noise over $K$ iterations, and dispatches only a prefix of the chunk before it plans again.

::: {#fig-diffusion-policy-architecture fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Diffusion policy architecture**: A continuous trajectory diffusion policy for visuomotor control, denoising a candidate action chunk from Gaussian noise across $K$ iterations and dispatching only a prefix of it before re-planning. Asynchronous buffering and an independent high-rate permission path can separate slower chunk generation from actuation. Conditional denoising can represent alternative demonstrated paths without taking their direct-regression mean. (Adapted from Chi et al. [@chi2024diffusionpolicy])." fig-alt="Diffusion Policy architecture and closed-loop action chunk denoising. An authentic continuous trajectory diffusion architecture for visuomotor control. The policy conditions on an observation horizon of multi-camera images and robot state vectors. Starting from pure Gaussian noise, the noise-prediction backbone (parameterized as either a 1D Temporal Convolutional U-Net or a Time-Transformer) iteratively denoises a candidate action trajectory across diffusion iterations. The resulting action chunk spans a prediction horizon, from which an execution horizon is dispatched to real-time motor controllers before receding-horizon re-planning occurs. This decouples slow generative inference from high-rate motor actuation while allowing alternative action sequences to be sampled when the learned conditional distribution and data support them. (Adapted from Chi et al. [@chi2024diffusionpolicy])."}

#### Forward diffusion and variance scheduling

The forward diffusion process progressively corrupts a ground-truth demonstrated action chunk $\mathbf{A}^0 \sim q(\mathbf{A})$ with Gaussian noise across $N$ discrete timesteps (or continuous diffusion time $t \in [0, 1]$):
$$ q(\mathbf{A}^k \mid \mathbf{A}^{k-1}) = \mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{A}^k; \sqrt{1 - \beta_k} \mathbf{A}^{k-1}, \beta_k \mathbf{I}\right) $$
where $\{\beta_k \in (0, 1)\}_{k=1}^N$ denotes a predefined variance schedule. Defining $\alpha_k = 1 - \beta_k$, the one-step transition evaluates to:
$$ \mathbf{A}^k = \sqrt{\alpha_k} \mathbf{A}^{k-1} + \sqrt{1 - \alpha_k} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{k-1}, \quad \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{k-1} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}) $$
Unrolling this recursion for $k = 2$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}^2 &= \sqrt{\alpha_2} \left( \sqrt{\alpha_1} \mathbf{A}^0 + \sqrt{1 - \alpha_1} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_0 \right) + \sqrt{1 - \alpha_2} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_1 \\
&= \sqrt{\alpha_2 \alpha_1} \mathbf{A}^0 + \sqrt{\alpha_2(1 - \alpha_1)} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_0 + \sqrt{1 - \alpha_2} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_1
\end{aligned}
$$
Because the linear combination of two independent zero-mean Gaussian random variables $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma_a^2 \mathbf{I})$ and $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma_b^2 \mathbf{I})$ is itself a Gaussian with variance $(\sigma_a^2 + \sigma_b^2)\mathbf{I}$, the combined variance of the noise terms simplifies algebraically:
$$ \alpha_2(1 - \alpha_1) + (1 - \alpha_2) = \alpha_2 - \alpha_1 \alpha_2 + 1 - \alpha_2 = 1 - \alpha_1 \alpha_2 $$
Defining the cumulative variance product $\bar{\alpha}_k = \prod_{s=1}^k \alpha_s$, mathematical induction establishes the closed-form marginal distribution at any arbitrary diffusion step $k$ directly from clean action chunk $\mathbf{A}^0$:
$$ q(\mathbf{A}^k \mid \mathbf{A}^0) = \mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{A}^k; \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_k} \mathbf{A}^0, (1 - \bar{\alpha}_k) \mathbf{I}\right) $$
allowing immediate sampling of noisy trajectories during training without simulating intermediate Markov chain transitions:
$$ \mathbf{A}^k = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_k} \mathbf{A}^0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_k} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}, \quad \boldsymbol{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}) $$

#### Reverse denoising and score-matching objective

The generative reverse process synthesizes an action trajectory from pure Gaussian noise $\mathbf{A}^N \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$ by parameterizing the conditional reverse transition distribution $p_\theta(\mathbf{A}^{k-1} \mid \mathbf{A}^k, \mathbf{O})$:
$$ p_\theta(\mathbf{A}^{k-1} \mid \mathbf{A}^k, \mathbf{O}) = \mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{A}^{k-1}; \boldsymbol{\mu}_\theta(\mathbf{A}^k, \mathbf{O}, k), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k\right) $$
By Bayes' rule, the true reverse posterior conditioned on the clean trajectory $\mathbf{A}^0$ is tractable and Gaussian: $q(\mathbf{A}^{k-1} \mid \mathbf{A}^k, \mathbf{A}^0) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A}^{k-1}; \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_k(\mathbf{A}^k, \mathbf{A}^0), \tilde{\beta}_k \mathbf{I})$, where:
$$ \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_k(\mathbf{A}^k, \mathbf{A}^0) = \frac{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{k-1}} \beta_k}{1 - \bar{\alpha}_k} \mathbf{A}^0 + \frac{\sqrt{\alpha_k}(1 - \bar{\alpha}_{k-1})}{1 - \bar{\alpha}_k} \mathbf{A}^k $$
Because $\mathbf{A}^0$ is unobserved at test time, the reverse process substitutes an estimate of $\mathbf{A}^0$ derived from Tweedie's formula.

For any Gaussian perturbation $\mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_0, \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_d)$ with prior density $p(\mathbf{x}_0)$, the conditional observation density is:
$$ p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{x}_0) = \frac{1}{(2\pi \sigma^2)^{d/2}} \exp\left( -\frac{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0\|^2}{2\sigma^2} \right) $$
Differentiating with respect to the noisy measurement $\mathbf{x}$:
$$ \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{x}_0) = -\frac{\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0}{\sigma^2} p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{x}_0) $$
The marginal density of noisy observations evaluates to $p(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{x}_0) p(\mathbf{x}_0) \, d\mathbf{x}_0$. Differentiating under the integral sign:
$$ \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} p(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{x}_0) p(\mathbf{x}_0) \, d\mathbf{x}_0 = -\frac{1}{\sigma^2} \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0) p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{x}_0) p(\mathbf{x}_0) \, d\mathbf{x}_0 $$
Dividing both sides by the marginal density $p(\mathbf{x})$:
$$ \frac{\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} p(\mathbf{x})}{p(\mathbf{x})} = \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} \ln p(\mathbf{x}) = -\frac{1}{\sigma^2} \left( \mathbf{x} - \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \mathbf{x}_0 \frac{p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{x}_0) p(\mathbf{x}_0)}{p(\mathbf{x})} \, d\mathbf{x}_0 \right) = -\frac{\mathbf{x} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_0 \mid \mathbf{x}]}{\sigma^2} $$
Multiplying by $\sigma^2$ and isolating $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_0 \mid \mathbf{x}]$ proves **Tweedie's formula**:
$$ \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_0 \mid \mathbf{x}] = \mathbf{x} + \sigma^2 \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} \ln p(\mathbf{x}) $$
Tweedie's formula reveals that the Bayes-optimal reconstruction of clean state $\mathbf{x}_0$ equals the corrupted measurement $\mathbf{x}$ shifted along the marginal Stein score $\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} \ln p(\mathbf{x})$ scaled by noise variance $\sigma^2$.

Rewriting the forward diffusion marginal $\mathbf{A}^k = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_k} \mathbf{A}^0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_k} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}$ as $\frac{\mathbf{A}^k}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_k}} = \mathbf{A}^0 + \frac{\sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_k}}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_k}} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}$, the effective noise variance is $\sigma^2 = \frac{1 - \bar{\alpha}_k}{\bar{\alpha}_k}$. Tweedie's formula directly equates the estimated clean trajectory $\hat{\mathbf{A}}^0$ and the Stein score $\nabla_{\mathbf{A}^k} \ln p(\mathbf{A}^k \mid \mathbf{O})$:
$$ \nabla_{\mathbf{A}^k} \ln p(\mathbf{A}^k \mid \mathbf{O}) = -\frac{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{A}^k, \mathbf{O}, k)}{\sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_k}} $$
Substituting $\hat{\mathbf{A}}^0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_k}} \left( \mathbf{A}^k - \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_k} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{A}^k, \mathbf{O}, k) \right)$ into the posterior mean $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_k$ reparameterizes the reverse transition mean:
$$ \boldsymbol{\mu}_\theta(\mathbf{A}^k, \mathbf{O}, k) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_k}} \left( \mathbf{A}^k - \frac{\beta_k}{\sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_k}} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{A}^k, \mathbf{O}, k) \right) $$
The noise-prediction network $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta$ is optimized via the simplified $L_2$ denoising score-matching objective:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{k \sim \mathcal{U}\{1, N\}, \boldsymbol{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}), (\mathbf{O}, \mathbf{A}^0) \sim \mathcal{D}} \left[ \left\| \boldsymbol{\epsilon} - \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta\left(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_k}\mathbf{A}^0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_k}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}, \mathbf{O}, k\right) \right\|^2 \right] $$
By following the score function $\nabla_{\mathbf{A}^k} \ln p(\mathbf{A}^k \mid \mathbf{O})$, reverse diffusion steers stochastic sampling toward high-density demonstration modes rather than averaging incompatible modes into an obstacle collision.

#### Continuous flow matching and vector field regression

While standard diffusion models formulate generation as reverse stochastic differential equations (SDEs), **continuous flow matching** [@lipman2022flow] generates trajectories along deterministic probability flows defined by ordinary differential equations (ODEs):
$$ \frac{d\mathbf{x}_t}{dt} = v_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t, \mathbf{O}) $$
The continuous vector field $v_\theta$ drives a source noise distribution $p_0(\mathbf{x}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$ to the empirical demonstration target distribution $p_1(\mathbf{x}) = q(\mathbf{x})$ across continuous time $t \in [0, 1]$, governed by the **continuity equation**:
$$ \frac{\partial p_t(\mathbf{x})}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left( p_t(\mathbf{x}) v_t(\mathbf{x}) \right) = 0 $$
Under an optimal transport conditional probability path, the continuous trajectory interpolates linearly between source noise $\mathbf{x}_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$ and demonstration chunk $\mathbf{x}_1 \sim \mathcal{D}$:
$$ \psi_t(\mathbf{x}_0) = (1 - t) \mathbf{x}_0 + t \mathbf{x}_1, \quad t \in [0, 1] $$
The conditional velocity along this straight optimal-transport path is constant across time:
$$ v_t(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{x}_1) = \frac{d}{dt} \psi_t(\mathbf{x}_0) = \mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{x}_0 $$
and the trajectory acceleration vanishes identically: $\frac{d^2}{dt^2} \psi_t(\mathbf{x}_0) = \mathbf{0}$.

The **Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) theorem** [@lipman2022flow] proves that regressing a neural vector field $v_\theta$ against this conditional vector field over paired samples $(\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_1)$ has gradients identical to regressing against the intractable marginal velocity field $u_t(\mathbf{x})$:
$$ \nabla_\theta \mathbb{E}_{t, \mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_1} \left[ \| v_\theta(\psi_t(\mathbf{x}_0), t, \mathbf{O}) - (\mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{x}_0) \|^2 \right] = \nabla_\theta \mathbb{E}_{t, \mathbf{x} \sim p_t} \left[ \| v_\theta(\mathbf{x}, t, \mathbf{O}) - u_t(\mathbf{x}) \|^2 \right] $$
The network is therefore trained via direct mean squared regression:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 1], \mathbf{x}_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}), \mathbf{x}_1 \sim \mathcal{D}} \left[ \left\| v_\theta\left((1 - t)\mathbf{x}_0 + t\mathbf{x}_1, t, \mathbf{O}\right) - (\mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{x}_0) \right\|^2 \right] $$
Because optimal-transport flow matching produces straight trajectories in state space with zero path acceleration ($\frac{d^2 \psi_t}{dt^2} = \mathbf{0}$), numerical integration truncation errors are drastically lower than in curved diffusion paths. In standard diffusion, the forward Brownian noise process induces high curvature in the probability flow ODE, requiring $K = 16\text{--}100$ steps to avoid veering off the data manifold. In contrast, straight probability flows allow low-order numerical solvers (such as a 2-step Euler integrator, $K=2$) to evaluate candidate trajectories with high fidelity. From a systems perspective, evaluating $K=2$ steps rather than $K=16$ slashes off-chip DRAM weight transfers by an order of magnitude (e.g., from $1.536\text{ GB}$ down to $192\text{ MB}$ per chunk for a $96\text{ MB}$ model), dropping generation latency to $15\text{--}20\text{ ms}$ and enabling synchronous closed-loop execution within real-time control deadlines.

#### Denoising steps against the control deadline

In continuous generative policies, the number of reverse evaluation steps $K$ is the governing systems lever trading off policy expressiveness at the physical plant against computational latency on accelerator hardware.

The reverse trajectory discretizes a continuous probability flow ODE or reverse SDE. Discretizing this path across $K$ finite steps introduces numerical integration errors:

- **Policy expressiveness:** Large step counts ($K \in [16, 100]$ in standard DDPM or accelerated DDIM samplers) minimize cumulative truncation error along non-linear score trajectories. This high resolution allows the generative process to navigate complex, non-convex score landscapes, faithfully preserving sharp multimodal separations (such as branching left or right around an obstacle) and tight assembly tolerances. Truncating $K$ aggressively (e.g., $K \le 4$ without distillation or flow matching) introduces severe discretization error, causing generated trajectories to collapse toward the empirical mean, clip physical obstacle boundaries, or produce high-frequency setpoint jitter that excites joint resonances.
- **Computational latency and roofline limits:** Crucially, reverse diffusion is an inherently sequential Markov chain: evaluation $k-1$ strictly requires the tensor output of evaluation $k$. Denoising steps cannot be parallelized across the time dimension on GPU or NPU accelerators. Total chunk generation latency scales linearly with $K$:[^fn-ml-denoising-latency]
  $$ \tau_{\text{inf}}(K) = t_{\text{vis}} + K \cdot t_{\text{step}} $$
  where $t_{\text{vis}}$ is the one-time visual feature extraction latency per chunk and $t_{\text{step}}$ is the forward execution time of noise-prediction network $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta$.
  On batch size 1 (single-robot closed-loop inference), matrix-vector multiplications exhibit low arithmetic intensity. Streaming network weights $\mathbf{W}$ of size $M_{\text{weights}}$ from off-chip DRAM takes time at least $t_{\text{stream}} = M_{\text{weights}} / \text{BW}_{\text{DRAM}}$. If arithmetic intensity $I = \text{FLOPs} / M_{\text{weights}} < \text{Peak FLOP/s} / \text{BW}_{\text{DRAM}}$, inference is strictly memory-bandwidth bound. For a $48\text{M}$-parameter model ($96\text{ MB}$ at FP16) on an embedded accelerator with $204.8\text{ GB/s}$ memory bandwidth, transferring weights once takes at least $0.469\text{ ms}$; executing $16$ sequential evaluations requires at least $7.5\text{ ms}$ of memory transfer alone before counting kernel launch latencies and activation memory traffic.

A physical robot's low-level joint controllers require fresh setpoints at a deterministic control loop period $\Delta t_{\text{ctrl}}$ (e.g., $20\text{ ms}$ for $50\text{ Hz}$ control). When a multi-step sampler's inference latency exceeds this period ($\tau_{\text{inf}} > \Delta t_{\text{ctrl}}$), synchronous lockstep execution is physically impossible: the controller starves while waiting for the accelerator, causing torque drops or unmodeled deceleration.

Physical AI architectures resolve this fundamental latency-expressiveness trade-off through three coordinated mechanisms:

1. **Action chunking:** The policy predicts a multi-step trajectory chunk $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{H_a \times D_a}$ spanning prediction horizon $H_a$. Executing an execution horizon $H_e \le H_a$ amortizes the $K$-step generation latency over $H_e \Delta t_{\text{ctrl}}$ of physical robot motion.
2. **Straight probability flows:** Continuous flow matching [@lipman2022flow] straightens probability trajectories, allowing low-order numerical solvers (such as a 2-step Euler integrator, $K=2$) to achieve distributional expressiveness comparable to a 16-step diffusion model, shrinking compute time to fit within synchronous control deadlines.
3. **Dual-rate asynchronous decoupling:** The application processor runs the generative denoising loop asynchronously at a relaxed rate ($10\text{--}20\text{ Hz}$), depositing action chunks across the proposal boundary into a lock-free single-producer single-consumer (SPSC) ring buffer. A dedicated safety microcontroller executes synchronously at $1\text{ kHz}$, interpolating spline knots, enforcing slew-rate limits, and gating commands through deterministic control barrier functions (@sec-boundary-machine-model).

@Algo-diffusion-policy-trajectory formalizes this dual-rate pipeline in the two-processor implementation, and @fig-diffusion-denoising-process illustrates the decoupling. @Sec-training-synthesis-regimes uses the timing budget below to evaluate which sampler fits the control deadline.

[^fn-ml-denoising-latency]: **Diffusion Denoising Latency Budget**\index{Diffusion sampling latency!sequential evaluation}: Sequential reverse diffusion cannot parallelize across sampling steps because each input requires the previous step's output. Total inference time $\tau_{\text{inf}} = t_{\text{vis}} + K t_{\text{step}}$ scales linearly with step count $K$, making step reduction or asynchronous chunking essential for real-time actuation.

```pseudocode
#| label: algo-diffusion-policy-trajectory
#| pdf-line-number: true
#| pdf-right-comment: false
#| html-comment-delimiter: "▷"

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Diffusion Policy Trajectory Chunk Denoising and Dual-Rate Actuation}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require observation history buffer $\mathbf{O}_t = (\mathbf{o}_{t-H+1}, \dots, \mathbf{o}_t)$, noise prediction network $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta$, noise schedule $\{\alpha_k, \bar{\alpha}_k, \sigma_k\}_{k=1}^{N_{\text{diff}}}$, chunk horizon $K$, safety microcontroller loop period $\Delta t_{\text{mcu}}$
\Ensure line-rate joint torque setpoint / action vector $\mathbf{a}_t$
\Statex
\State \textbf{Application Processor: Asynchronous Trajectory Chunk Generation ($10\text{--}20\text{ Hz}$)}
\State $\mathbf{E}_t \gets \Call{VisualEncoder}{\mathbf{O}_t}$
\State $\mathbf{A}^{N_{\text{diff}}} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}_{K \times D_a})$ \Comment{initialize reverse diffusion from Gaussian noise}
\For{$k = N_{\text{diff}}$ \textbf{down to} $1$}
    \State $\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}} \gets \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{A}^k, \mathbf{E}_t, k)$
    \State $\boldsymbol{\mu}_k \gets \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_k}} \left( \mathbf{A}^k - \frac{1 - \alpha_k}{\sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_k}} \hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}} \right)$
    \State $\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$ \textbf{if} $k > 1$ \textbf{else} $\mathbf{z} \gets \mathbf{0}$
    \State $\mathbf{A}^{k-1} \gets \boldsymbol{\mu}_k + \sigma_k \mathbf{z}$
\EndFor
\State $\mathbf{A}_{\text{chunk}} \gets \mathbf{A}^0$
\State $\Call{DepositSpscRingBuffer}{\mathbf{A}_{\text{chunk}}}$ \Comment{lock-free deposit into shared buffer}
\Statex
\State \textbf{Safety Microcontroller: Synchronous Deterministic Actuation ($1\text{ kHz}$)}
\If{$\Call{HasNewChunk}{\text{SPSC}}$}
    \State $\Call{UpdateSplineKnots}{\text{SPSC}}$
\EndIf
\State $\mathbf{a}_{\text{raw}} \gets \Call{CubicSplineInterpolate}{\mathbf{A}_{\text{chunk}}, t_{\text{current}}}$
\State $\Delta \mathbf{a} \gets \Call{clamp}{\mathbf{a}_{\text{raw}} - \mathbf{a}_{\text{prev}}, -\dot{\mathbf{a}}_{\max} \Delta t_{\text{mcu}}, +\dot{\mathbf{a}}_{\max} \Delta t_{\text{mcu}}}$ \Comment{kinematic slew-rate governor}
\State $\mathbf{a}_{\text{clamped}} \gets \mathbf{a}_{\text{prev}} + \Delta \mathbf{a}$
\State $\mathbf{a}_t \gets \Call{SafetyGovernorClamp}{\mathbf{a}_{\text{clamped}}}$ \Comment{deterministic envelope enforcement}
\State $\Call{TransmitPwmRegisters}{\mathbf{a}_t}$
\State $\mathbf{a}_{\text{prev}} \gets \mathbf{a}_t$
\State \Return $\mathbf{a}_t$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
```

::: {#fig-diffusion-denoising-process fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Diffusion policy action chunk denoising and receding-horizon decoupling**: (a) Multimodal resolution: direct regression with mean squared error averages divergent demonstrations into an invalid obstacle collision, whereas diffusion policy stochastically selects a coherent demonstrated mode. (b) Iterative trajectory denoising: starting from Gaussian noise $\mathbf{A}^K \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$, reverse diffusion progressively resolves a coarse trajectory into a smooth action chunk $\mathbf{A}^0$. (c) Dual-rate decoupling: an asynchronous neural planner on the application processor populates a lock-free ring buffer, feeding a $1\,\text{kHz}$ safety microcontroller executing deterministic spline interpolation and safety clamping. (Adapted from Chi et al. [@chi2024diffusionpolicy])." fig-alt="Three-panel schematic of Diffusion Policy action chunk denoising and receding-horizon decoupling. (a) Multimodal resolution showing failure of regression mode averaging vs. stochastic mode selection. (b) Iterative trajectory denoising across reverse diffusion steps from pure noise to a smooth action chunk. (c) Dual-rate asynchronous decoupling between a 15 Hz application-processor neural planner, an SPSC ring buffer, and a 1 kHz safety microcontroller that runs the permission path."}
